links.note: The church of Rus' was a province of the church of Constantinople. Mouravieff, a Russian church historian writing in 1838, says its chief bishops were named at Constantinople and answered to the patriarch there. One of them, Matthew, was sent from the city just before the crusaders took it.

links.note: A Life of Nerses says he was made head of his church at Caesarea, in Cappadocia. It says the Armenians went there for this until the Council of Chalcedon. But Malachia Ormanian, a historian of their church, says Caesarea never ruled over it.
links.outcome: At Caesarea, many bishops met and made Nerses the head of the church of Great Armenia.

links.note: A Coptic history of the 700s describes the king of Makuria in Nubia. It says the patriarch in Egypt ordained his chief bishop, who then ordained the bishops and priests of the land. When that bishop died, the patriarch of Alexandria chose and ordained another.
links.outcome: The patriarch in Egypt named and ordained the chief bishop of Makuria, and chose a new one when he died.

links.note: Around 1200 a Coptic survey of Egypt's churches says the head bishop of Abyssinia is sent 'from the patriarch of Alexandria'. 'Abd al-Latif, writing in the same years, tells of an envoy from the Abyssinian king. The envoy reported the bishop's death and asked for a new one. A note in the Kebra Nagast names a Coptic book of 'the throne of Mark' in King Lalibela's time.

sources.work: Churches and Monasteries of Egypt, attributed to Abu Salih (trans. Evetts, 1895), on Abyssinia
sources.quote: A metropolitan is sent from the see of Mark the Evangelist to Abyssinia ^, from the patriarch of Alexandria in Egypt ;

links.note: In 1490 three Christians set out from India to ask the patriarch Simeon for bishops. He made two monks bishops and sent them back with the Indians. In 1504 a later group of bishops wrote to the patriarch from Malabar that its Christians had welcomed them.

sources.quote: In the year one thousand eight hundred and one of Alexander (a.D. 1490), three believing Christian men came from the remote countries of India to the Catholicos Mar Simeon, Patriarch of the East, in order to bring bishops to their countries.

links.note: Gregory wrote to all the bishops of Numidia, answering a request they had sent to his predecessor. He let them keep their old customs for choosing a senior bishop. But he barred bishops who had come over from the Donatists from that rank.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Register I.77, To all the Bishops of Numidia (NPNF 2.12, Barmby)
sources.quote: And we, indeed, according to the tenour of your representation, allow your custom (so long as it clearly makes no claim to the prejudice of the catholic faith) to remain undisturbed, whether as to constituting primates or as to other points;

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Register I.77, To all the Bishops of Numidia (NPNF 2.12, Barmby)

links.outcome: Pope Gregory let the Numidian bishops keep their old way to pick a head bishop, but not one who had been a Donatist.
links.change_reason: Outcome added (ruling 2): Gregory's letter sets a rule for another church's choice of its senior bishop. Nothing else changed.

links.note: An Observant chronicle says that in 1517 Pope Leo X issued two bulls for the Franciscans. One joined all the reformed friars into a single body. The other set terms between the head of the whole order and the head of the Conventual friars. The chronicle's editors wrote in 1887 that Leo had made two separate orders.
links.outcome: In 1517 Pope Leo X made the reformed friars one body under their own head, set apart from the Conventual friars.
